extracted.intended_audience: readers or writers of 19th-century nautical/gothic fiction; anyone interested in historical seamanship and shipboard mutiny tactics
extracted.subtask_description: A chunk of Edgar Allan Poe's nautical Gothic narrative describing mutiny, a violent gale, shipboard survival actions, and a deliberate deception (the corpse-apparition) used to retake a brig. Contains both dramatic narrative and practical seamanship/procedural details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lying-to in a gale — when and how
rubrics_metrics.description: “Lying-to, or, in sea-parlance, ‘laying-to,’ is a measure resorted to for various purposes... This being done, the bows point within a few degrees of the direction from which the wind issues... The helm is usually lashed down, but this is altogether unnecessary... the rudder has no effect upon the vessel when lying-to.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When used to ride out a gale (wind ahead or sea too heavy): bring head nearly to the wind so a chosen sail is drawn flat aft; common sail choices vary by vessel construction — the foresail is most usually employed (Grampus lay-to under a close-reefed foresail); large square-rigged ships use storm-staysails; the jib, jib+foresail, double-reefed foresail, after-sails, or foretopsails may be used depending on the craft. If the working sail tears, the vessel may fall off and be at the mercy of the sea, in which case you should put her before the wind and scud until other sail can be set. Helm need not be lashed tight (better loose to allow play and avoid rudder being torn off). Note: lying-to opens seams and can worsen leaks; when a vessel is leaky she is often put before the wind (scudded) even in heavy seas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency measures for a leaking/disabled vessel in heavy weather
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative descriptions of actions to keep a leaky brig afloat: continuous pumping, use of improvised sails/thrummed sail under the bows, cutting away masts, lightening by jettisoning wreck and bodies, and attention to ballast and rigging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain pumps continuously (e.g., one pump going at all times or on a set rotation). Use a sail thrummed under the bows to aid in keeping water at bay. If leak gains, consider scudding rather than lying-to because straining while lying-to opens seams. To reduce strain and righting moments, cut away masts (mainmast or foremast) when necessary to lighten and stabilize the hull — prepare stays and lanyards and time the cuts with a lee-lurch. Remove weight and wreckage (throw bodies and damaged boats overboard) and lighten stowage. Watch for shifted ballast: if ballast shifts to leeward the vessel may list dangerously and pumps may be ineffective. Be aware of structural vulnerabilities (e.g., the heel of a mast stepped between decks can lead to imminent failure). These are desperate, high-risk measures: cutting away masts may leave the vessel a hulk and expose her to further seas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting vigilance/suspicion among a crew (signs a surprise will fail)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicators that the mate or crew are on the alert: presence of a watch on deck while lying-to (unusual unless discipline is strict), missing tools (axes, handspikes) from customary places, muskets or arms laid ready, and altered crew behaviour (quarrels, divided parties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat a deck watch during a gale and the absence of usual tools as strong evidence that the officers suspect particular individuals; this makes direct surprise risky. Assess alliances among crew (who has joined the mate vs. cook or other factions) before attempting bold actions. If suspicion is suspected, avoid simplistic ambush plans and instead seek strategies that exploit psychological vulnerabilities (e.g., superstition) or wait for a genuinely unanticipated moment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deception by corpse-apparition to paralyze and retake a vessel
rubrics_metrics.description: The plan and execution for impersonating a corpse (Rogers) to terrify a superstitious crew: use the victim's distinctive smock, construct a false swollen stomach and stuffed hands, apply white chalk to the face, blotch with blood, reproduce distinctive marks (streak across the eye), and exploit the dim, swinging light and tempestuous conditions to enhance believability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare the disguise using recognizable clothing of the corpse (unique smock/stockinett), stuff bedclothes to emulate a swollen stomach, pad hands (mittens stuffed with rags), apply white chalk for pallor and use blood for blotches and characteristic marks. Time the apparition to coincide with extreme weather, darkness/dubious light, and a crew already psychologically primed (recent sight of the real corpse, superstitious conversation, isolation from other ships). Have associates take preliminary actions (remove watch quietly, create a plausible pretext for one man’s absence, position lookouts) and place improvised weapons (pump-handles) near the companion-way. The strategy: present the apparition to paralyze the crew, then immediately exploit the confusion — rush in silently, secure exits (companion-way), use available arms (pump-handles, stools, muskets) to subdue key opponents, and be prepared for violent resistance from those who recover their wits. Note cautions: if there is a vigilant watch or ample means of clear daylight inspection, the deception may fail; success depends on limited means of verifying the apparition, the crew’s superstitions, and the environmental conditions (gale, swinging lantern light).
